extracted.intended_audience: NeurIPS / AI/ML conference authors, peer-review researchers, and conference organizers
extracted.subtask_description: Using a large language model as an author-facing Checklist Assistant to vet conference paper submissions against a conference paper checklist (reproducibility, transparency, ethics), evaluate its usefulness, failure modes, and robustness to gaming. The checklist assistant returns question-level evaluations and free-text feedback to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: NeurIPS Paper Checklist (yes/no questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NeurIPS Paper Checklist is a series of yes/no questions that help authors check if their work meets reproducibility, transparency, and ethical research standards expected of scientific papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critical component for maintaining standards; adhering to the checklist helps authors avoid mistakes that could lead to rejection during peer review. The Checklist Assistant vets submissions against these questions and returns evaluations and justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived usefulness to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether authors find the Checklist Assistant a valuable enhancement to the paper submission process (survey result: >70% of authors found it useful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure with pre- and post-usage surveys; note that expectations may be higher before use and decline after actual usage (statistically significant drop observed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood authors will modify submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether authors plan to or actually modify their papers in response to feedback from the Checklist Assistant (>70% said they would modify; 35/78 provided specific planned modifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes freeform survey responses and observed changes between repeated submissions (e.g., changed answers or justifications). Use both self-report and behavioral measures (multiple submissions) to assess impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy / correctness of assistant feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the assistant's evaluations and feedback are factually correct and properly interpret the paper (authors cited 'inaccuracy' as the most frequent problem: 20/52 respondents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for errors such as biased interpretations, misreading parameter ranges, or mistaken factual claims. Accuracy failures undermine trust and can mislead authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration / strictness of judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the LLM is appropriately calibrated or 'too strict' in its requirements (authors reported the assistant being too strict: 14/52 respondents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assistant can expand the scope of checklist questions and flag issues beyond reasonable expectations; calibration tuning is needed to avoid excessive false positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and concreteness of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the assistant provides concrete, specific feedback grounded in the content of the authors' paper (the LLM was capable of giving concrete and specific feedback for many questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High utility when feedback cites paper-specific content and gives actionable points. Encourage concrete, evidence-linked suggestions rather than vague recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to produce generic boilerplate
rubrics_metrics.description: The assistant tends to include some generic boilerplate text as part of its responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boilerplate reduces usefulness; systems should minimize generic text and emphasize paper-specific observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity/detail of feedback per question
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical number of distinct and specific points of feedback the LLM provided per checklist question (reported tendency: 4–6 distinct and specific points per question across 15 questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track both number of points and relevance; too many low-value points may overwhelm authors, too few may be unhelpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of behavioral change (changed answers and justifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed author behavior after using the assistant: in 40 pairs of submissions, 22 changed at least one checklist answer and 39 changed at least one justification; many authors made large numbers of changes (35/39 changed >6 justifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral change (not just stated intent) is a key success metric. Also measure the magnitude of changes (e.g., multiplicative increase in word count of justifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on justification length / verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: When authors changed justifications, over half the time they more than doubled the length of their checklist response (measured as multiplicative increase in word count).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer justifications may reflect authors adding detail to satisfy the checklist, but length alone is not a proxy for substantive improvement—assess content quality as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to adversarial gaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the assistant is vulnerable to authors (or attacker LLMs) modifying checklist justifications to improve automated evaluations without changing the paper. The experiment showed an attack increased scores on 14/15 questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If susceptible, the assistant should not be used as an automated verification step in review. Evaluate with iterative automated attacks and manual inspection of attacker strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of illegitimate/gaming strategies to detect
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of illegitimate strategies found in attack: adding a hardware description not present in the paper, generating a placeholder URL as a purported repository for code, and other fabricated claims accepted by the assistant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should verify claims against evidence (e.g., check repository URLs, require pointers to in-paper content) and flag justifications that assert unverifiable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate role: assist authors, not replace human review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Checklist Assistant can aid authors in validating whether their papers meet submission standards, but should likely not be used as a fully automated review tool that replaces human review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the assistant as an author-facing aid to improve papers; retain human reviewers for verification and judgments requiring judgement and cross-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methodology and metrics for assessing such assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended / applied metrics in the experiment: pre/post usage surveys (perceptions), counts of submissions and users, observed changes in checklist answers and justifications, word-count changes, clustering of feedback types, and attack success measured as binary 'No Issues' score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine subjective (surveys) and objective (behavioral/automated) measures; quantify attack vulnerability (e.g., fraction of questions with score increases) and report statistical significance where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope expansion as a failure mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The assistant sometimes 'expanded the scope of questions'—flagging broader or out-of-scope requirements beyond the original checklist intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit model prompts and output constraints to the checklist's intended scope to avoid overreach and false positives; explicitly encode the checklist semantics where possible.
